text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's Austrian newspapers:
- Telecoms companies Verbund and OeBB want to buy a fifty percent stake in Wiener Telekabel to strengthen their unit Tele.ring and they are looking for a foreign partner.

- The dominant Social Democrat Party wants to bring the foreign ministry into investigations into the 1989 murder of three Kurds in Vienna. However, it opposes the setting up of a parliamentary inquiry committee on the issue.

- Gerhard Praschak, former secretary of ex-chancellor Franz Vranitzky and board director at Kontrollbank, committed suicide on the weekend after another ex-minister Rudolf Scholten became a board member and he felt his position was threatened.
- Women's Minister Barbara Prammer wants preferential treatment for firms that further women.
- Agriculture Minister Wilhelm Molterer said ahead of a European Union gene summit that more research into the health risks of genetically engineered products was needed.
- International fraud in Europe is costing citizens and businesses in the EU up to 820 billion schillings annually. A lack of international cooperation and the Internet are to blame, the paper says.
- The European Commission plans in three months time to look at the future of nuclear energy plants in eastern Europe.
- President Thomas Klestil said in a radio interview on the weekend that he would not make any decision about running for a second term in forthcoming presidential elections until late autumn.
- A gene summit beginning on Monday will be the acid test for direct democracy in Austria, say environmentalists.

- European Union Director Benavides Salas is threatening to take action against tricks played by Austria's energy sector as he says he opposes the Austrian model of risk-sharing planned with the opening up of the market.
